title: How To Signal For Your Students' Attention
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin explains why two popular attention-getting methods — silent hand signals and counting down aloud from five — fall short, focusing particularly on countdowns, which he argues sound threatening, tend to slow down over time as teachers give students more leeway, and implicitly accept a delayed response as good enough. His alternative is a single, simple auditory cue, such as a verbal phrase or a distinctive sound, expected to produce immediate attention. He lays out an eight-step teaching sequence for installing the signal: explaining it plainly, modeling it through role-play, having students practice it during a distracting activity, reviewing it daily for several weeks, praising early success, using 'do it again' when the response falls short, scoring student performance to build motivation, and eventually testing it in whispered form. He frames the seemingly minor skill of quickly securing attention as one that transfers to excellence in everything else students do.
points: Counting down aloud to get attention is discouraged because it sounds threatening, tends to slow over time, and accepts delayed compliance.
A single, consistent auditory signal, explicitly taught and practiced, produces faster and more reliable attention than gradual countdowns.
The eight-step teaching sequence (explain, model, practice, review, praise, do it again, score, whisper-test) mirrors how any classroom procedure should be installed.
Treating this small procedural skill with rigor is presented as a model for the level of excellence expected in everything students do.
quotes: To students, it sounds like a threat. It’s like saying, “You better look at me before I finish counting, or else.” Classroom management doesn’t need to be negative to be effective. In fact, it works better if it isn’t.
The count, then, becomes slower over time, a slippery slope indeed. We want students to become better, quicker, more attentive. Not less.
Counting down amounts to accepting less than what students are capable of. It also encourages selective hearing.
One of the keys to great classroom management is to never move on until you get exactly what you want from your students.
Is it worth putting so much effort into something so rudimentary? Yes, yes, and yes. Like so much of classroom management, this exercise in excellence will transfer to everything they do.
